questions.stem: Roughly how many countries have French as an official language?
questions.explanation: French is official in around 29 countries across Europe, Africa, the Americas and the Pacific. It is one of very few languages spoken as an official language on every inhabited continent.

questions.stem: Which of these Pacific territories has French as an official language?
questions.explanation: New Caledonia is a French territory, as is French Polynesia — both are closer to Australia than most French-speaking places, which makes French a regional language as well as a European one.

questions.stem: On which continent do the most French speakers live today?
questions.explanation: Africa has by far the largest number of French speakers, and the gap is growing with population. Assuming France is the centre of the French-speaking world is a common and out-of-date picture.

questions.stem: Which Canadian province has French as its official language?
questions.explanation: Quebec is officially French-speaking, and Canada as a whole is officially bilingual. Quebec French has its own vocabulary and accent, in the same way Australian and British English differ.

questions.stem: What does « la Francophonie » refer to?
questions.explanation: « La Francophonie » is the international organisation and community of French-speaking states. The lower-case « francophone » simply describes a French speaker.

questions.stem: Which greeting suits a teacher you have just met?
questions.explanation: « Bonjour » with « madame » or « monsieur » is the safe formal greeting. « Salut » and « coucou » are for friends, and using them with a teacher would read as over-familiar rather than friendly.

questions.stem: What does choosing « vous » rather than « tu » signal?
options: That the sentence is in the past tense
That the speaker is asking a question
Respect or distance, or that you are addressing more than one person
questions.explanation: « Vous » does two jobs: it is the plural 'you', and it is the polite singular. English lost this distinction, so it has to be learned as a social judgement rather than translated.

questions.stem: In France, what is « la bise »?
options: A greeting of light kisses on the cheek
A formal handshake used in business
A written form of address in letters
questions.explanation: « La bise » is a common greeting between friends and family, and the number of kisses varies by region. It is not universal and not used in every situation, which is why watching what others do matters.

questions.stem: Why do French speakers say « J'ai faim » rather than 'I am hungry'?
options: « Être » does not exist in the present tense
« Faim » is a verb rather than a noun
It is an old form no longer used in speech
French uses « avoir » for states English treats with 'to be'
questions.explanation: French treats hunger, thirst, cold, fear and age as things you *have*. This is a genuine structural difference between the two languages, and the kind of comparison UL03 asks students to notice and describe.

questions.stem: What is a 'false friend' in language learning?
options: A word with more than one meaning
A word that is difficult to pronounce
A word that looks the same in two languages but means something else
A word borrowed directly from another language
questions.explanation: « Librairie » looks like 'library' and means bookshop; « actuellement » looks like 'actually' and means currently. False friends are dangerous precisely because they look easy.

questions.stem: Which French word has been borrowed into English unchanged?
questions.explanation: English has borrowed enormously from French since 1066 — café, restaurant, menu, ballet, genre. That shared vocabulary is a real advantage for an English speaker learning French, as long as false friends are watched for.

questions.stem: What is a cognate?
options: A word that has no translation in the other language
A word invented by learners of the language
A word that is spelled the same but pronounced differently
A word that looks similar in two languages and shares its meaning
questions.explanation: « Table », « animal » and « important » are cognates between French and English. Spotting them is a genuine reading strategy — a French text is far less opaque than it first looks.

questions.stem: How does French show politeness in a request differently from English?
options: By putting the verb at the end
By using the conditional, as in « je voudrais »
questions.explanation: English softens with 'please' or 'could I'; French shifts the verb into the conditional. « Je veux un café » is grammatically fine and socially abrupt, which is the sort of thing grammar alone will not tell you.

questions.stem: Why is « Comment vous appelez-vous ? » more suitable than « Tu t'appelles comment ? » with a stranger?
options: It is the only grammatically correct version
It is shorter and therefore more polite
It uses the formal « vous » and full inversion
It is in a different tense
questions.explanation: Both are correct French. The first is formal in two ways at once — « vous » and inversion — while the second is informal in both. Register in French is carried by grammar, not just by word choice.

questions.stem: What does it mean that French nouns have grammatical gender?
options: Only nouns for people and animals have gender
Gender changes depending on the speaker
Every noun is masculine or feminine regardless of meaning
questions.explanation: « Le livre » is masculine and « la table » feminine with no logic to recover. English has no equivalent, so the article has to be learned as part of the word rather than worked out.

questions.stem: Which statement about French in Australia is accurate?
options: It is one of the most commonly taught languages in Australian schools
It is an official language of Australia
It is spoken as a first language by most Australians
It is taught only at university level
questions.explanation: French is among the languages most widely offered in Australian schools, alongside Japanese, Italian, Chinese and Indonesian. Australia has no official language declared in law at all.

questions.stem: On which continent is French an official language in the largest number of countries?
questions.explanation: More than twenty African countries use French officially, a legacy of colonial administration. Europe has far fewer.

questions.stem: Which of these countries has French as an official language?
questions.explanation: Senegal uses French in government and schooling alongside Wolof and other national languages.

questions.stem: Which European country other than France has French as an official language?
questions.explanation: Belgium has three official languages: Dutch, French and German. Switzerland and Luxembourg also use French officially.

questions.stem: How many official languages does Switzerland have?
questions.explanation: German, French, Italian and Romansh. Which one you meet depends entirely on which canton you are in.

questions.stem: What is the capital of Quebec province?
questions.explanation: Montreal is the larger city but Quebec City is the capital. Ottawa is the national capital and sits in Ontario.

questions.stem: Which Pacific territory near Australia uses French officially?
questions.explanation: New Caledonia is a French territory about three hours from Brisbane, which makes French a near neighbour language for Australians.

questions.stem: Which greeting would you use to a shopkeeper in the afternoon?
questions.explanation: « Bonjour » covers the whole day until evening. « Salut » is for friends and « bonne nuit » is said when going to bed.

questions.stem: What should you say when entering a small French shop?
questions.explanation: Greeting the shopkeeper on entry is expected rather than optional, and not doing it reads as rudeness.

questions.stem: What does « Bonsoir » replace, and when?
questions.explanation: The switch happens around six o'clock. « Bonne nuit » is only for someone going to sleep.

questions.stem: What does « s'il vous plait » mean?
questions.explanation: « S'il te plait » is the « tu » version. The politeness is carried by the pronoun inside the phrase.

questions.stem: What is the usual reply to « merci »?
questions.explanation: « De rien » means 'it is nothing'. « Je vous en prie » is the more formal equivalent.

questions.stem: Which French word has entered English unchanged?
questions.explanation: Kindergarten is German, piano is Italian and tsunami is Japanese. English has taken thousands of words from French since 1066.

questions.stem: Which English word came into the language from French after 1066?
questions.explanation: The animals kept their English names and the meat took French ones, because the people eating it spoke French.

questions.stem: What does the false friend « librairie » mean?
questions.explanation: A library is « une bibliotheque ». Assuming the obvious cognate is exactly the trap a false friend sets.

questions.stem: What does the false friend « actuellement » mean?
questions.explanation: 'Actually' is « en fait ». The two words look identical and mean different things.

questions.stem: What does the false friend « sensible » mean in French?
questions.explanation: 'Sensible' in English is « raisonnable ». This pair catches people in both directions.

questions.stem: What does « assister a » mean?
questions.explanation: « J'ai assiste au concert » means I attended the concert. To help someone is « aider ».

questions.stem: What does the greeting « Salut » signal about the relationship?
options: It is used only in writing
It is used only at night
questions.explanation: « Salut » works for both hello and goodbye among friends. Using it with a stranger or a teacher is too familiar.

questions.stem: When is « la bise » usually exchanged?
questions.explanation: The number of kisses varies by region, which is why visitors find it hard to judge. It is for people you know.

questions.stem: What is the currency used in France?
questions.explanation: France replaced the franc with the euro in 2002. Switzerland still uses Swiss francs, so the answer depends on which French-speaking country.

questions.stem: Which of these is a French-speaking African country?
questions.explanation: Kenya and Ethiopia use English and Amharic; Angola uses Portuguese. The colonial history of each country decided the official language.

questions.stem: Which country has the largest number of French speakers in Africa?
options: The Democratic Republic of the Congo
questions.explanation: The DRC has more French speakers than France itself on some counts, and the balance is still shifting towards Africa.

questions.stem: What is the national day of France?
questions.explanation: Le quatorze juillet marks the storming of the Bastille in 1789. Calling it 'Bastille Day' is an English habit rather than a French one.

questions.stem: How are dates written in French?
questions.explanation: « Le 14 juillet » — day first, like Australia and unlike the United States. Months are not capitalised.

questions.stem: Which of these is written without a capital letter in French?
options: The first word of a sentence
questions.explanation: Days, months, languages and nationalities as adjectives all stay lowercase: « lundi », « juillet », « le francais ».

questions.stem: How would you write 'Monday 3 March' in French?
questions.explanation: Both the day and the month stay lowercase, and the day number comes before the month.

questions.stem: What does « une ecole primaire » correspond to in Australia?
questions.explanation: « Le college » is the first part of high school and « le lycee » the senior years, which is why « college » is a false friend.

questions.stem: What does « le college » mean in France?
questions.explanation: It covers roughly Years 7 to 10. Australian 'college' meaning university does not transfer.

questions.stem: Which meal is « le petit dejeuner »?
questions.explanation: Literally 'the little lunch'. « Le dejeuner » is lunch and « le diner » is the evening meal.

questions.stem: Why does French say « J'ai quinze ans » rather than 'I am fifteen'?
options: French treats age as something you have
Fifteen is a noun in French
questions.explanation: Age uses « avoir » with the word « ans ». Saying « je suis quinze » makes no sense to a French ear.

questions.stem: What does it tell you that French has both « courriel » and « email »?
options: Languages borrow and also invent alternatives
French has no word for email
Email is not used in French
questions.explanation: « Courriel » was coined in Quebec and is used officially; « email » is common in everyday France. Both are current.

questions.stem: What is the role of « la Francophonie »?
options: Linking countries that share the French language
questions.explanation: It is an international organisation of member states, not a language authority. That job belongs to the Academie francaise.

questions.stem: Which accent changes the sound of the letter e in « ete »?
questions.explanation: « E » with an acute accent is pronounced like the 'ay' in 'day'. The cedilla belongs under a c.

questions.stem: What does the cedilla under « c » in « francais » do?
options: Makes the c sound like k
Makes the c sound like s
questions.explanation: Without it, a c before a, o or u would be a hard k sound. The cedilla keeps it soft.

questions.stem: Why is French taught widely in Australian schools?
options: It is the closest language to English
It is required by the curriculum
It has the most speakers worldwide
It is a major world and diplomatic language
questions.explanation: French is an official language of the UN, the EU and the Olympic movement, and New Caledonia is a near neighbour.

questions.stem: What does « bon appetit » do that English has no phrase for?
options: Marks the start of a meal
questions.explanation: It is said to everyone at the table before eating. English has no direct equivalent, which is why it is borrowed.

questions.stem: Which of these is a formal way to close a letter in French?
questions.explanation: « Cordialement » is the standard email sign-off. The others are for friends, and « bisous » means kisses.

questions.stem: What does « vouvoyer » mean?
questions.explanation: Its partner « tutoyer » means to use « tu ». English lost this distinction centuries ago.

questions.stem: Who usually decides when a pair switches from « vous » to « tu »?
options: It is decided by age alone
The older or more senior person
questions.explanation: Being invited to « tu » is a small social event. Jumping to it uninvited is presumptuous.

questions.stem: Which statement about regional languages in France is accurate?
options: Breton and Occitan are spoken alongside French
French is the only language ever spoken in France
questions.explanation: Breton, Occitan, Basque, Corsican and Alsatian all survive, though French is the sole official language.

questions.stem: What does « le metro » refer to?
questions.explanation: Short for « le chemin de fer metropolitain ». The Paris system opened in 1900 and the word has since spread worldwide.

questions.stem: What is a cognate, in language learning?
options: A word with a shared origin in two languages
A word that has changed meaning
questions.explanation: « Table » and 'table' are cognates. A false friend looks like a cognate and has drifted in meaning.

questions.stem: Roughly what proportion of English vocabulary has French or Latin roots?
questions.explanation: Estimates vary, but a very large share of English words arrived through French or Latin, which is why so many look familiar.

questions.stem: Why do French speakers often find English spelling difficult?
options: English spelling is less consistent with its sounds
English has more letters in its alphabet
questions.explanation: French spelling has silent letters too, but its rules are more regular. English draws spellings from several languages at once.

questions.stem: Which statement about French films in Australia is accurate?
options: They are always dubbed into English
They are shown only on television
They are usually shown with subtitles
questions.explanation: Subtitling keeps the original performance, which is why it is preferred for cinema releases.

questions.stem: What does the phrase « Je ne sais quoi » mean when used in English?
questions.explanation: Literally 'I do not know what'. English borrowed it whole because it had no compact way to say the same thing.

questions.stem: What is « le TGV »?
questions.explanation: « Train a grande vitesse ». It links French cities at speeds well above anything running in Australia.

questions.stem: Which country was the first to make French an official language outside Europe?
questions.explanation: French settlement in what became Quebec began in the early seventeenth century, and French remains official there today.

questions.stem: What does it mean that a language is 'pluricentric'?
options: It is spoken in one country only
It is used only for business
It has more than one standard form
questions.explanation: French has recognised standards in France, Quebec and elsewhere. So does English, which is why Australian and American spelling differ.

questions.stem: Why might a French speaker say « Je voudrais » rather than « Je veux » in a shop?
options: It is the only correct form
It is required after a greeting
questions.explanation: « Je veux » is grammatical but blunt. The conditional softens a demand into a request, exactly as 'I would like' does.

questions.stem: Which is the polite way to get a stranger's attention?
questions.explanation: « Pardon » or « excusez-moi » opens politely. « Viens » is an informal command and would be rude to a stranger.

questions.stem: What does the Academie francaise do?
questions.explanation: Founded in 1635, it issues a dictionary and recommendations. It has no power to compel anyone to follow them.

questions.stem: Why do Quebec and France sometimes use different words for the same thing?
options: Quebec borrowed all its words from English
The two varieties developed separately for centuries
Quebec French is a different language
questions.explanation: Quebec was cut off from France after 1763 and has also resisted English borrowings more actively, giving « fin de semaine » for « week-end ».

questions.stem: What does « la rentree » refer to?
options: The return to school and work after summer
The end of the school year
questions.explanation: La rentree in early September is a national moment in France, covered in the news the way the start of a season is here.

questions.stem: Which statement about French spoken in Africa is accurate?
options: It is identical to French in France
It is only used in writing
It has its own vocabulary and accents
questions.explanation: African varieties have distinctive vocabulary and pronunciation, and a growing share of the world's French speakers.

questions.stem: What does it mean to say a French noun has grammatical gender?
options: Gender shows up only when the noun is plural
Every noun is masculine or feminine, whatever it means
Only nouns for people and animals carry a gender
The speaker chooses the gender to suit the sentence
questions.explanation: « Le livre » and « la table » have no natural gender at all. The article has to be learnt with the noun.

questions.stem: Why is « merci » sometimes a refusal in French?
options: It changes meaning with the accent
Said when offered more, it can mean 'no thank you'
It only means no in writing
questions.explanation: Offered a second helping, « merci » on its own often declines. « Oui, merci » accepts, and the difference matters at a table.

questions.stem: What does the tricolore flag of France stand for?
questions.explanation: The motto dates from the Revolution and appears on public buildings across France.

questions.stem: Which sport has strong French vocabulary in its international use?
questions.explanation: Fencing uses « en garde », « touche » and « riposte » internationally, because the modern sport was codified in France.

questions.stem: What does « bonne chance » mean?
questions.explanation: « Chance » in French means luck, not opportunity — another false friend hiding inside a common phrase.

questions.stem: Which statement about learning French in Australia is accurate?
options: It is the most widely spoken home language here
It is never taught before the first year of high school
It is offered only in independent schools
It is among the most commonly taught school languages
questions.explanation: French is widely offered in Australian schools, though Mandarin, Italian and Japanese are also common.

questions.stem: What does the expression « avoir le mal du pays » mean?
questions.explanation: Literally 'to have the sickness of the country'. French builds many feelings with « avoir » where English uses 'to be'.

questions.stem: Why is it worth learning set phrases as whole units?
options: They are spelt the way they are pronounced
They are the only phrases that use accents
They are built from one word each
They often break the rules you have learnt
questions.explanation: « Il y a », « avoir faim » and « bon appetit » cannot be assembled from grammar rules, so they are learnt whole.
